beats.scene: COLD OPEN — Two Pairs of Hands
beats.summary: Night, interior of Saltwick Light. Extreme close-ups only: Orla's salt-cracked hands trimming a wick, striking a match on the third try, cranking a heavy six-turn mechanism while a boy's smoother hands mimic the motions half-heartedly beside hers. Over this, the only narration of the episode, a three-card legend: 'A hundred years ago, in one night, the sea left. / The law says every light burns till dawn. / Nobody remembers why.' On the last card we pull wide for the first time — the beam sweeping over an ocean of nothing: salt flats, stone kelp, a whale's ribcage catching the light. Espen yawns, framed small against the enormous absence.

Match cut from the lamp's flame to dawn sun cresting the cliff edge. The beam clicks off; the title assembles out of drifting salt motes in the morning light. Silence except wind and one gull that has never seen water.

beats.scene: The Boy Who Sells the Sea
beats.summary: Morning village life on the cliff top: laundry lines, a rope-elevator down to the flats, and Espen hawking scavenged trinkets — fossil kelp, a ship's doorknob, chips of saltglass — to Hulda, the oil merchant, who weighs them against the coins she's owed for lamp oil. Hulda, counting slowly so he can see: 'Your gran burns a month of my oil to light a sea that isn't there.' Espen doesn't defend the lamp — he agrees, grinning, and pockets a coin he skims off Orla's oil payment for himself. Turn: we learn the light is bleeding the household dry, and Espen is quietly stealing from it.

Afternoon, the keeper's kitchen and lamp room — the warm heart of the episode. Orla makes Espen run the lighting drill 'again': dry the matches on the stove ledge, six turns to wake her, six to keep her, count the dark between the sweeps. He recites her rhyme in a mocking singsong; she deadpans that he got it right, which annoys him more. What he doesn't see, and we do: her hand spasms and drops a match, she folds a spotted handkerchief into her sleeve, and when his back is turned she holds the table to stay upright. Turn: the drill isn't habit — it's a handoff, and she knows it.

Dusk gathering. Espen announces he's asked Hulda for a place on her next caravan — real work, real money, anywhere but here. Orla doesn't argue, doesn't forbid; she slides the keeper's ledger across the table, a century of entries in dead relatives' handwriting, her own the last, shakier every page — and says only, 'Sign out properly when you go. Keepers sign.' He storms out to the cliff stairs. On the windowsill behind him, unnoticed by anyone, his jar of saltglass has begun to glow a faint, cold blue. Turn: she has released him, which is the one thing he didn't want, and the episode's danger has already started.

Storm front swallowing the last light as Espen sulks back up the tower — and finds Orla collapsed on the spiral stairs, six steps from the lamp room, oil can still in her hand, the sun already gone. He tries to haul her down toward her bed; her grip on his wrist is the strongest thing in the scene. She can't manage sentences, only the subtitled fragments: 'Light first.' 'Then me.' 'Count.' Turn: for the first time in his life she needs him, and she spends that need on the lamp instead of herself — which he cannot yet forgive or understand.

beats.scene: SETPIECE — Six Minutes of the Wrong Sea
beats.summary: BIGGEST SETPIECE. Alone in the lamp room, Espen fails: matches damp because he skipped the stove-ledge step, wind through a pane he never fixed, his hands shaking into an exact echo of hers from the cold open. The jar in his pocket blazes blue — and in its glow, in reflections on the glass and in one wide held shot, we see the Dry Sea filling: darkness moving like tide, vast slow whale-shadows with faint fin-lights rising up the cliff face toward the village's few lit windows, which float like buoys. The Undertow is never centered, never explained — pressure on the ears, frost of salt creeping over the balcony rail, the jar's light the only thing keeping the lamp room 'above water.' On the sixth minute he does it her way — rhyme whispered through his teeth, six turns, flame — and the beam sweeps out; the dark peels off the rocks below like water off a withdrawing wave. Turn: the museum piece is a seawall, and he is standing on it.

The rest of the night in intercut fragments: Espen cranking on the count, then down six steps to wipe Orla's face, then back up before the mechanism runs out — a boy pacing the exact rhythm the rhyme was built to teach. He sets the glowing jar on her sill like a night-light; she surfaces once, touches it, and says, 'Your grandfather kept weather in jars too. He never believed it either. Then he did.' He starts to ask what's out there; she's already asleep, or pretending. He doesn't wake her. He goes back up and counts. Turn: the handoff completes without either of them naming it — he stops keeping the light for her and starts keeping it because of what he saw.

Dawn. Espen performs the extinguishing ritual alone and correctly — wick, vents, glass wiped in circles, the way her hands did it in the cold open, now his. Down in the waking village he returns the skimmed coin to Hulda and instead of apologizing asks the price of a month of oil, then two. Hulda studies him — the salt frosted white on his shoulders, the burn on his thumb — and for once doesn't make the joke. Turn: the village skeptic recalibrates; the boy who sold the sea is buying it back.

Espen, hollow-eyed on the tower balcony, hears it before he sees it: small bells, out of rhythm with the wind. Far below, a single figure walks the Dry Sea out of the dawn haze — wide hat, long coat sewn with dozens of tiny bells, a printed license plate hung at the chest: a Bellfarer, the first crosser Espen has ever seen. From the flats, the figure looks up at the lit-then-dark lamp, then at the boy, and calls up the episode's last dialogue: 'Whose light is this now?' Espen glances back at Orla's window — the saltglass jar still faintly blue on her sill — and answers, 'Mine.' The Bellfarer: 'Good. The light across the strait went dark three weeks ago. I've come to ask what you're going to do about it.'

Hold on the strait: far across the exposed seabed, a sister tower stands on the opposite cliff, dark, tiny, wrong. In the salt at the Bellfarer's feet, half-buried, a chip of saltglass glows — pointing across. Card: 'Next — The Far Shore Is Listening.'

hook_ending: The Bellfarer — bells, hat, license — arrives at dawn and makes Espen say 'Mine' out loud, converting the night's private handoff into a public vow before delivering the hook: the sister lighthouse across the strait has been dark for three weeks. The question isn't 'what's out there' (Espen now knows); it's 'what are you going to do about it' — duty escalating from holding one light to answering for another.
why_it_works: Every genre beat is load-bearing for the relationship: the cold open's hand-doubling pays off when Espen's shaking hands become hers in the setpiece; the mocked rhyme becomes the survival tool; the skimmed coin becomes the dawn restitution; the ledger 'sign out' becomes 'Mine.' Keeping the Undertow to roughly ninety seconds of oblique screen time (reflections, pressure, one wide shot) makes the six dark minutes terrifying on the engine's actual strengths — light, silhouette, sound — while spending the runtime where an audience bonds: two people who love each other lying to each other gently. The grief is pre-paid — Orla survives the night, but the show and the viewer both know what the handoff meant — so episode 1 lands as emotional realism, not a fridging. Subtitle load stays light (~170 events) because chores, weather, and counting carry whole scenes silently, and it rewards rewatching: the glowing jar in beat 5, Orla's dropped match, and the six-steps-from-the-top staging all read differently once you know.
risks: The trade-off is spectacle: viewers expecting a monster-forward premiere get ninety seconds of creature, mostly reflected — if the setpiece's sound design and jar-light staging under-deliver, the episode reads as slow. Orla surviving the episode softens the immediate stakes (mitigated by making her decline visibly irreversible). The six-minute failure must be timed honestly or the rhyme/count motif feels decorative. And the Bellfarer's two-line hook carries the entire serialized pull — if 'Whose light is this now?' lands flat in subtitle-only delivery, the ending is quiet twice in a row (dawn ritual, then hook), so the bells and the dark sister tower must do the propulsion visually.
